stem.en: An antibiotic that jams bacterial ribosomes is prescribed for an infection. Kabir says "so it stops all protein-making in the body". Why is that wrong, and where is there a risk?

text.en: Human ribosomes have a different shape and are not jammed, so the body's proteins are made as usual. The risk is the mitochondria: their ribosomes are bacterial in shape, from their history in Book VIII, and some antibiotics touch them, which is why a few have side effects.

feedback.en: If it did, the patient would die in hours. It fits one shape and not the other.

text.en: It only works on the infection because bacteria are smaller.

feedback.en: Size of the cell is not it. The ribosome's slot is shaped differently.

text.en: It works on any cell without a nucleus.

feedback.en: The nucleus has nothing to do with it. The ribosome's shape does.

explanation.en: Ask which molecule the drug fits. If it fits the bacterial ribosome and not the human one, it is selective. If it also fits mitochondrial ribosomes, expect side effects.
